content: 1. The duration of treatment with ceftazidime/avibactam is typically 7 to 14 days. Renal function should be carefully monitored in patients over 65 years of age. Dosage adjustments for elderly patients should be based on renal function as outlined in the dosage modifications section. 2. Coadministration of the cholera vaccine with systemic antibiotics should be avoided, as antibiotics may be active against the vaccine strain. Patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination should not receive the cholera vaccine. 3. Ceftazidime/avibactam may reduce the efficacy of microbiota oral formulations due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents can decrease the efficacy of microbiota oral products, which contain bacterial spores. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2 to 4 days before initiating microbiota oral therapy. 4. Ceftazidime/avibactam increases the toxicity of aminoglycosides such as amikacin, gentamicin, kanamycin, neomycin, plazomicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Caution should be exercised, and close monitoring is recommended. Cephalosporins may enhance the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides. 5. Ceftazidime/avibactam may reduce the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors, including atezolizumab, avelumab, balstilimab, camrelizumab, cemiplimab, cosibelimab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, penpulimab, retifanlimab, sintilimab, tislelizumab, and toripalimab, through an unspecified interaction mechanism. Caution should be exercised, and close monitoring is advised. 6. Probenecid increases the levels of ceftazidime/avibactam by decreasing renal clearance. Coadministration is not recommended as per prescribing information. In vitro studies show that probenecid inhibits the uptake of avibactam by OATP1 and OATP3 transporters in the kidney by 56-70%, potentially reducing renal elimination of avibactam. 7. Ceftazidime/avibactam may increase the toxicity of voclosporin through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Coadministration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may increase the risk of acute and/or chronic nephrotoxicity. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. 8. Common adverse effects of ceftazidime/avibactam include diarrhea (8%), nausea (7%), vomiting (5%), headache (3%), dizziness (2%), and abdominal pain (1%). Other reported adverse effects include rash, infusion site phlebitis, constipation, pruritus, and upper abdominal pain. 9. Blood and lymphatic disorders associated with ceftazidime/avibactam include thrombocytopenia, thrombocytosis, leukopenia, aplastic anemia, prolonged prothrombin time, hemorrhage, and pancytopenia. General disorders include injection site phlebitis. Infections such as candidiasis have been reported. Laboratory investigations may show increased levels of aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase. 10. Metabolic and nutritional disorders include hypokalemia. Nervous system disorders include dysgeusia. Renal and urinary disorders include acute kidney injury, renal impairment, nephrolithiasis, and toxic nephropathy. Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders include rash, maculopapular rash, and urticaria. Psychiatric disorders include anxiety. Gastrointestinal disorders include colitis and hepatic dysfunction, including cholestasis. 11. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis and severe skin reactions, have been reported with beta-lactam antibacterials. Caution is advised in patients with a history of allergy to cephalosporins, penicillins, or carbapenems. Cross-sensitivity among beta-lactam antibacterials is established. Discontinue the drug if an allergic reaction occurs. 12. Neurological adverse effects, including seizures, nonconvulsive status epilepticus, encephalopathy, coma, asterixis, neuromuscular excitability, and myoclonia, have been reported with ceftazidime, particularly in patients with renal impairment. Dosage adjustments should be made based on creatinine clearance (CrCl). 13. Ceftazidime/avibactam should only be prescribed for confirmed or strongly suspected bacterial infections to avoid the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of resistance. 14. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies of ceftazidime/avibactam, ceftazidime, or avibactam in pregnant women. Animal studies indicate that neither ceftazidime nor avibactam was teratogenic in rats at doses 40 and 9 times the recommended human clinical dose, respectively. In rabbits, at twice the exposure seen at the human clinical dose, no teratogenic effects were observed.
